newsitem.title: USA: U.S. campaign funds probe fails to produce evidence.
newsitem.headline: U.S. campaign funds probe fails to produce evidence.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Two weeks of hearings into fund raising in 1996 U.S. political campaigns have produced tantalizing circumstantial evidence but no proof that U.S. national security was compromised.
This week, the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee will switch its focus from Democratic to Republican misdeeds, with former Republican chairman Haley Barbour expected to testify.

So far, the political effects of the hearings, which Democrats feared would be a major embarrassment, seem negligible. The subject matter is complex, the names unfamiliar and television networks are largely uninterested.
That may change later this year when the committee focuses on the role of Vice President Al Gore, seen as the leading Democratic contender for the presidency in 2000.

A CBS poll last week found that 77 percent of respondents thought Republicans and Democrats used the same fund-raising techniques. Only 12 percent said they were "very interested" in the hearings; 38 percent said they were "somewhat interested" and the rest were either not very interested or completely uninterested.

The hearings have centred on the activities of John Huang, an Asian American who worked for the Indonesian-based Lippo Group, a sprawling conglomerate with close ties to the Chinese government and a long friendship with President Bill Clinton dating to when he was governor of Arkansas.

In 1994 Huang became a mid-level official at the U.S. Commerce Deptartment, apparently more because of his record as a Democratic Party supporter than his qualifications for the job. In that position, he had access to classified information while retaining close ties to his former employers.

In early 1996 Huang moved across to the Democratic National Committee as a fund-raiser where he collected more than $1.6 million which was subsequently returned when it was demonstrated that it came from illegal foreign sources.
Though there is much that looks strange or even sinister in Huang's complex web of relationships, Republican investigators have failed to unearth a final piece of evidence that would seal the case.
"We can follow money in the United States and back to whichever foreign bank it came from. But after that, the trail runs dry. We can't get to the ultimate source," said one committee official.
Likewise, the suggestion that Huang passed sensitive information he learned at the Commerce Department to Lippo, or to the Chinese.

The committee can trace the hundreds of phone calls Huang made while at Commerce, many from a secret office across the street, to Lippo officials but it does not know what was discussed. It knows the dates of his visits to the Chinese embassy but it cannot establish whom he met or what he said.

Making its task more difficult, the committee does not have complete access to intelligence, which is being reviewed by the Justice Department with a view to beginning criminal proceedings against Huang and other key players.
Mississippi Republican Sen. Thad Cochran, a member of the committee, said he suspected Attorney General Janey Reno was playing politics by withholding the information.
History shows that investigations of this kind only command wide public credibility when Republicans and Democrats succeed in working together and forging a consensus.

There is no sign of that happening in this investigation. Democrats, with the sole exception of Connecticut Sen. Joseph Lieberman, have acted as virtual defence attorneys, focusing on what witnesses do not know rather on what they do and taking pains to point out the lack of concrete proof.
"It's fair to say that from the reviews so far, this has been a bust. They still need to show where the evidence is. Where's the beef? There's nothing there," said Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle.
